question: Does rendering text as an image cost fewer or more tokens than the text itself, for a vision model reading it back — and does the answer generalise across content types?

methods.textTokens: REAL — Anthropic's /v1/messages/count_tokens endpoint, called server-side with a live subscription token (never exposed to this page or printed anywhere), same model as the vision read.
methods.imageTokensFormula: Anthropic's published estimate: ceil((width_px * height_px) / 750). Cited, not invented. https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/vision
methods.imageTokensReal: REAL — the same count_tokens endpoint, called with the actual rendered PNG as an image content block. This is the gold-standard number; the formula above is reported alongside it as the documented estimate, not used in place of it.
methods.renderer: A plain monospace canvas renderer (kernel-backed layout math in kernel.mjs, witness-gated), black text on white, 16px font unless noted, word-wrapped to a fixed max width. No stylistic tuning in either direction.
methods.fidelity: A vision read (Claude Sonnet 5, native vision) of the rendered PNG, transcribed and compared against ground truth.

contaminationControl.risk: For content the experimenter (Kar) authored or already knew, a 'correct' vision read could be memory rather than genuine vision — the source was already in context.
contaminationControl.design: A held-out set (10 rows of {word, 4-digit code}) was generated by a seeded script (gen-holdout.mjs) whose console output never printed the actual values — only a row count and the seed. The plaintext was never read by Kar before the vision read. The rendered image was viewed FIRST, the transcription recorded, and ONLY THEN was ground-truth.json opened to compare.
contaminationControl.appliesTo: the 'holdout' row only. The 'prose' and 'structured' rows are NOT contamination-controlled — Kar wrote both, so their fidelity results are a weaker, secondary confirmation (the render/legibility pipeline works), not evidence about faithful reading of unknown content.

results.description: A genuine paragraph of ordinary English prose (a kestrel hunting a vole), 387 characters, 6 lines rendered.
results.fidelity: exact match (visual inspection) — CONTAMINATED, Kar authored this text

results.description: Real repo/witness/test/fuzz facts from tonight's own builds, key=value shaped, 415 characters, 8 lines rendered.
results.fidelity: exact match (visual inspection) — CONTAMINATED, Kar authored this text

results.description: 10 rows of {random word from a 12-word list, random 4-digit code}, seed 20260923, generated by script, never seen as plaintext by Kar before the vision read.
results.fidelity: 10/10 EXACT MATCH — genuine cold vision read, contamination-controlled (see contaminationControl above)

secondaryFinding: Anthropic's published (w*h)/750 formula UNDERESTIMATED the real measured image token cost in all 3 samples, by 5.0% to 13.7%. Small sample (n=3), but consistent in direction — worth budgeting a margin above the formula, not treating it as exact.

verdict.headline: It depends on how efficiently the content tokenizes as TEXT, not on visual repetition per se — and the effect is modest, not dramatic, in these samples.
verdict.detail: Ordinary prose (387 chars, 2.71 chars/token) comes out roughly break-even as an image, marginally WORSE (+2.1%) — prose is already close to a general-purpose BPE tokenizer's native efficiency, so rendering it as pixels buys nothing and costs a little. Content that tokenizes poorly as text because of its symbolic shape (repeated '=', '/', mixed alphanumeric codes — NOT because it is 'repetitive' in a visual sense) can come out ahead as an image: the hand-written structured sample saved 22.9%, and the contamination-controlled random holdout set saved 4.6% while achieving perfect fidelity. Image token cost is purely a function of rendered pixel area (Anthropic's own formula has no content-awareness at all); text token cost is highly content-shape-dependent. The crossover is not about 'repetition compresses visually' — it is about which of the two very different cost functions is cheaper for a GIVEN content shape, at the minimum pixel density needed to stay legible.
verdict.generalises: No, not as a universal law from 3 samples — but the MECHANISM (text-tokenizer inefficiency vs content-agnostic pixel cost) is a real, identifiable axis, not a fluke of one dataset. Framed against compression-is-the-intelligence (Hutter): this is a case where the 'compressor' being compared against (Claude's own BPE tokenizer) is already near-optimal for one content class (prose) and measurably suboptimal for another (symbol-heavy structured text) — the image path doesn't compress better in any absolute sense, it just doesn't inherit the tokenizer's specific blind spot. That is a narrower, more honest claim than 'images compress text.'
verdict.hypothesisCheck: Kar's original hypothesis ('prose fails, structured/repetitive might not') is DIRECTIONALLY correct in these 3 samples, but the reason given in kar-pixelfold's README (Zipf's-law-flavoured 'visual repetition') was imprecise — the real driver identified here is text-tokenizer efficiency per content shape, not visual redundancy. Corrected, not just confirmed.

reproduce: 1. node count-tokens.mjs <path-to-content.json>  (si-didy/count-tokens.mjs — requires a live Claude subscription/API credential, resolved server-side via auth.mjs, never exposed)
2. Render content with render-harness.html's window.__render(text, {fontPx, maxWidthPx}) to get {width, height, dataUrl}
3. Wrap the dataUrl's base64 payload in an image content block and pass to count-tokens.mjs for the real image-token count

4. For a contamination-controlled fidelity check: node gen-holdout.mjs (regenerates ground-truth.json + holdout-text.txt with the same seed, byte-identical), render, view the image WITHOUT reading the plaintext file first, transcribe, then diff against ground-truth.json
